t: One-command install scripts for every OS
title: One-command install scripts for every OS
description: Text Generation WebUI ships one-command installer scripts: start_linux.sh, start_windows.bat, start_macos.sh, and start_wsl.bat. Running the script creates a conda-style installer directory, downloads the right PyTorch build, and installs the requirements, so the whole UI is up after a single command. The installer/ folder keeps the Python environment isolated from the system Python, which is why reinstalls and updates stay clean.

demo.expected_output:
1. ./start_linux.sh
2. installer created
3. requirements installed
4. UI at 127.0.0.1:7860
done: text-generation-webui ready

t: Chat, instruct, and notebook interface modes
title: Chat, instruct, and notebook interface modes
description: The interface has three main modes. Chat mode runs multi-turn conversations with characters. Instruct mode takes an instruction and an input, like a classic prompt-completion playground. Notebook mode gives a free-form text box for raw generation. A mode dropdown at the top switches instantly, and generation parameters (temperature, top_p, top_k, repetition penalty) live in a shared parameters panel so tuning applies across modes.

demo.program:
modes={'chat':'multi-turn conversations','instruct':'instruction + input','notebook':'free-form generation'}
for m,d in modes.items(): print(m,'->',d)
demo.expected_output:
chat -> multi-turn conversations
instruct -> instruction + input
notebook -> free-form generation

t: Model loaders: llama.cpp, ExLlamaV2, Transformers and more
title: Model loaders: llama.cpp, ExLlamaV2, Transformers and more
description: The Model tab offers many loaders because no single backend is best for every card. Transformers runs anything but is slowest. llama.cpp and llama-cpp-python run quantized GGUF models on CPU or mixed GPU. ExLlamaV2 is the fast GPTQ/EXL2 CUDA loader. AutoGPTQ and AutoAWQ load their quantized formats. Choosing the loader that matches the model file format is the single most important setting in the UI.

title: The models/ directory layout
description: Everything the UI can load lives under predictable folders: models/ holds model weights (organized per model in subfolders), loras/ holds LoRA adapters, presets/ holds YAML generation presets, characters/ holds character cards, extensions/ holds UI extensions, training/ holds datasets and LoRA outputs, and css/ holds custom styling. Knowing this layout lets you install a model by simply dropping a folder into models/ and refreshing the Model tab.

title: OpenAI-compatible API mode
description: Launching with the --api flag exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST API alongside the web UI, so any OpenAI client library can talk to the local model by pointing its base URL at the machine. There is also a --api-port and --api-key option, and the classic /v1/chat/completions endpoint works, which means local models drop into existing tooling with a one-line URL change.

demo.program:
print('python -c "from openai import OpenAI; c=OpenAI(base_url=\'http://127.0.0.1:5000/v1\', api_key=\'x\')"')
print('endpoint: /v1/chat/completions -> local model')

title: Characters and generation presets
description: The Character tab loads character cards (YAML files with name, greeting, and context) that define who you are talking to, while presets/ holds generation presets: named bundles of sampler settings tuned for chat, creative writing, or code. Users share characters and presets, so downloading one is a file copy into characters/ or presets/ followed by a refresh in the UI.

title: The extensions system
description: Extensions in extensions/ add features like text-to-speech (ElevenLabs, Coqui, Silero), speech-to-text (Whisper), translation, image generation, and the model downloader gallery. They are enabled with --extensions or toggled in the Session tab, and each extension can add its own UI tab. Because extensions are plain Python + Gradio code, writing one is the standard way to customize the UI.

title: Model downloader tab
description: The Model tab's Download sub-tab fetches models straight from the Hugging Face Hub by repository name, with checkboxes for which files to pull (useful for grabbing only the needed quantization). It writes into models/ automatically, so a new model is ready to load without leaving the browser. This is the fastest legal path from a model card to a running chat.

title: Quantization formats it understands
description: The UI exists largely to make quantized models usable: GPTQ (4-bit GPU), GGUF (llama.cpp CPU/GPU), AWQ (4-bit), EXL2 (ExLlamaV2 variable-bit), and plain fp16 Transformers checkpoints. Each format needs its matching loader, and the Model tab shows which loaders are compatible. Picking 4-bit quantization typically cuts VRAM to roughly a quarter with modest quality loss.

title: Instruction templates and chat templates
description: The Instruct-template dropdown controls how prompts are wrapped before generation (Alpaca, Vicuna, ChatML, Llama-2-chat, Mistral and dozens more). Picking the template that matches the model's training format is critical: a mismatched template produces rambling output even from a good model. The UI ships a large template library and lets users paste custom ones.

title: Token counter and generation stats
description: The UI shows live token counts, generation speed in tokens per second, and total VRAM usage while generating, which makes it a practical benchmarking bench: load the same prompt across two models or two loaders and compare tokens/sec directly. The log panel records the raw prompt after templating, so prompt bugs are visible instead of mysterious.

title: LoRA training tab
description: The Training tab fine-tunes models with LoRA/QLoRA on custom datasets: pick a base model, a dataset in training/datasets, set rank/alpha/learning-rate, and start training from the browser. Outputs land in training/loras/ ready to load in the Model tab. It is the simplest on-ramp to adapting a local model without writing training code.

title: Switching models without restarting
description: The Model dropdown lists every model folder under models/, and loading a different one unloads the current weights and loads the new ones in the same session. This makes A/B comparisons fast: keep the chat history, swap the model, and continue the same conversation to feel the difference. VRAM is the limit, so smaller quantizations swap fastest.

title: Essential command-line flags
description: Common flags: --listen exposes the UI on the network, --model preloads a model, --loader picks the backend, --extensions enables extensions at startup, --api turns on the API, --auto-launch opens the browser, --model-dir points at a custom models folder, and --verbose prints debug logs. Flags can also live in CMD_FLAGS.txt so the same launch is repeatable.

title: Fixing out-of-memory errors
description: When the GPU runs out of memory, the standard fixes in order are: use a smaller quantization (EXL2 4-bit instead of 8-bit), lower --n-gpu-layers so some layers run on CPU, reduce --max_seq_len / context length, or switch to the llama.cpp CPU-heavy loader. The UI's VRAM meter shows exactly how much each model needs, turning OOM from guesswork into arithmetic.

demo.program:
vram={'model':4.2,'ctx':1.1,'total':5.3}
print('needed VRAM GB:',vram['total'],'-> quantize or offload if over budget')
demo.expected_output: needed VRAM GB: 5.3 -> quantize or offload if over budget
